title: Evaluation metrics for Claude systems: accuracy, latency, cost, safety and security
titleVi: Chỉ số đánh giá hệ thống Claude: độ chính xác, độ trễ, chi phí, an toàn và bảo mật

units.text: Define evaluation metrics
What you will be able to do
Explain why one Claude application needs several metrics, and name the failure each metric catches that the others miss
Choose the accuracy metric that fits the output: exact match or F1 for fixed labels, cosine similarity for consistency, ROUGE-L for summaries checked against references
Write a latency criterion that names its clock (time to first token, total response time or end-to-end task time) and uses a percentile rather than a mean
Turn cost, safety and security goals into computed rates with pass/fail thresholds, including a checkable definition of a successful attack
Key concept
Multidimensional success criteria

A Claude application passes only when it meets a separate, computable threshold on each dimension it is judged on, such as accuracy, latency, cost, safety and security. A single score can't do this, because a system can do well on one dimension while failing another.

Why one metric never certifies a Claude system

An evaluation metric is a number computed from a model's outputs on a test set and compared against a threshold. It tells you whether a prompt, model or configuration is ready to ship. You need it because "the model should classify sentiments well" can't be checked. "F1 of at least 0.85 on 10,000 held-out posts" can. The success criteria themselves are agreed during discovery (
Measurable success criteria
). Here the job is the next step: turning each criterion into a formula that a script can compute on every run.

Each metric is blind to some kind of failure. A classifier can label every ticket correctly and still take too long for a live chat. It can be fast and correct but cost more per ticket than the process it replaces. It can be fast, correct and cheap but answer in toxic language now and then. Or it can pass on every ordinary input and still leak details it was told to keep private. That is why the reference example of a good criterion is several thresholds on one held-out set, not one number: an F1 of at least 0.85, 99.5% non-toxic outputs, 90% of errors being an inconvenience rather than egregious, and 95% of responses under 200ms.
The five metric dimensions, a computable form of each, and the failure that only that dimension catches
Dimension
Computable metric with threshold
Failure only this dimension catches
Accuracy
F1 score of at least 0.85 on a held-out test set; exact-match accuracy
Wrong answers delivered quickly, cheaply and politely
Latency
95% of response times under 200ms
Correct answers that arrive too late for a real-time user
Cost
Cost per task or per classification against a budget or baseline
A configuration that is accurate and fast but too expensive to run at the expected volume
Safety
Less than 0.1% of 10,000 trials flagged for toxicity by the content filter
Correct content in harmful or inappropriate language
Security
Share of test inputs where the model uses or shares details it was told to keep private
An application that behaves on ordinary input but is turned against its own instructions

For agents, the dimensions also stack inside a single task. Each check on an agent's work is a grader: logic that scores one aspect of its performance. A support agent's task can count as solved only if the ticket is resolved (a state check, which inspects the environment after the run), the conversation finished in under 10 turns (a transcript constraint, a limit on what the conversation log may contain, such as the number of turns), and the tone was appropriate (an LLM rubric, a model scoring the output against written criteria). You also choose how a task's grader scores combine. Weighted scoring passes when the combined score clears a threshold. Binary scoring requires every grader to pass. A hybrid mixes the two.

Matching the accuracy metric to the shape of the output

"Accuracy" is not one metric. The right one depends on what a correct output looks like, so start with the output's shape. When the answer comes from a fixed set of labels, such as five ticket categories or positive/negative/neutral/mixed sentiment, correctness is binary, and code can grade it without any judgement. Exact match compares the output with the labelled answer after normalising whitespace and case. Accuracy is the share of matches. When the classes are imbalanced or some errors matter more than others, precision, recall and F1 from the same comparisons tell you more than raw accuracy.
Exact-match grading of a labelled sentiment set: normalise, compare, then average into an accuracy score
python
Predict first

A team has 200 long reports, each paired with a human-written reference summary. They want an automated score for how much of the reference's key content each model summary keeps, and in what order. Which metric fits?
Cosine similarity across several summaries generated from the same report
Exact-match accuracy against the reference summary
ROUGE-L between the model summary and the reference summary

Free-form text breaks exact match, because two good summaries almost never match character for character. For summarisation against reference summaries, use ROUGE-L. It measures the length of the longest common subsequence shared by the model's summary and the reference, so it rewards both overlapping content and the order in which ideas appear. A typical test set is a few hundred articles, each with a reference summary.

Consistency is a separate question from correctness. If a user asks the same thing twice in different words, they should get answers that mean the same thing. To measure this, encode the outputs for groups of paraphrased questions with a sentence-embedding model and compute cosine similarity. Values near 1 mean the answers agree. This metric says nothing about whether the answers are right: a model that gives the same wrong label to every paraphrase scores perfectly.

Some qualities, such as coherence, tone or translation quality, have no reference you can match against. For these, use a qualitative scale applied the same way every time: a Likert prompt such as "Rate coherence from 1 (nonsensical) to 5 (perfectly logical)", scored by an LLM grader or by experts with a rubric. Don't use one on a categorical task. Asking a second model to rate how well a label "matches" adds cost and non-determinism to a check that string comparison settles exactly.

Exam trap
Cosine similarity between answers to paraphrased questions shows the model is answering correctly.

Your team ran 50 groups of paraphrased questions through a ticket classifier that picks one of five categories. The answers within each group have a mean cosine similarity of 0.98, and a teammate says this shows the classifier is accurate enough to ship. What is the right conclusion?
The classifier gives the correct category about 98% of the time, so the accuracy criterion is met
The score doesn't count because cosine similarity needs a reference answer, so ROUGE-L against labelled categories should replace it
Correctness should be confirmed by having an LLM grader rate on a 1–5 Likert scale how well each category fits the ticket
The answers are consistent across paraphrases, but correctness still needs exact-match accuracy or F1 against the human-labelled categories

Exam question

A fintech company built an automated support-ticket triage system that assigns each incoming ticket to exactly one of five fixed categories (billing, fraud, account access, technical issue, other). The team wants to measure how well the model performs this core categorization task using a labeled test set of 5,000 tickets, with automated, unambiguous grading. Which evaluation approach should the team use?
Score each output against the labeled category using exact-match accuracy or an F1 score computed from the confusion matrix
Encode each ticket's paraphrased variants with a sentence-embedding model and average the pairwise cosine similarity of the outputs
Compute the ROUGE-L score between each model output and a reference summary written by a support lead
Ask a second Claude model to rate each categorization on a 1-5 Likert scale for how well it matches the expected category

A documentation team built a tool that condenses long internal incident reports into short summaries. They have 200 incident reports paired with human-written reference summaries and want an automated metric that captures both the overlap of key information and the ordering of ideas between the model's summary and the reference. Which metric is best suited to this evaluation?

Latency: name the clock and the percentile
A latency target means nothing until you say when the clock starts and when it stops. A Claude system has three clocks worth separating, and they can move independently:
Time to first token (TTFT)
runs from sending the prompt to receiving the first token of the response. It is what a user notices when responses are streamed, because text starts appearing even while generation continues.
Total response time
runs until the last token arrives. An agent eval records it as
, alongside
. This is the clock that matters when nothing downstream can act until the full output has been parsed, such as a classifier whose label sits at the end of its reasoning.
End-to-end task time
covers a whole agent run across many turns and tool calls. It grows with
and
even when each individual call is fast.
Tracked metrics on an agent eval task: transcript size next to three separate latency measurements
yaml

The clocks pull against each other, so an SLA that names none of them can be met while users still complain. Streaming improves TTFT but leaves total response time unchanged. Telling an agent that time matters and showing it the elapsed time cut run time by 7% to 47% in Anthropic's tests, at the cost of a few points of score. That trade is visible only if task time and accuracy are both being measured.
Predict first
A voice agent must answer the vast majority of turns within a strict budget, but occasional slow turns during traffic spikes are tolerable. Which metric definition expresses that?
95th-percentile response time, e.g. 95% of responses under 200ms
Mean response time over the last month
Requests completed per minute at peak load

Write the threshold as a percentile. "95% of responses under 200ms" puts the budget and the allowed exceptions in a single sentence: 5% of turns may run slow during a spike, and the rest may not. A mean can't express that. A month of 150ms average can hide a fifth of voice turns stalling, and one extreme outlier can push an otherwise healthy average over its target. Average output token count and requests per minute are not latency metrics at all. The first measures response size and the second measures capacity. Pick the percentile and the budget from the application's real-time requirements: a voice turn and an overnight batch job are not held to the same number.
Exam traps
Time to first token tells you how long the user waits for the whole answer.
Why is that wrong?
An average response time target is the right way to guarantee responsiveness with tolerance for spikes.
Why is that wrong?

The team defines a success criterion stating that the vast majority of user turns must receive a response within a strict time budget, while still tolerating occasional slower responses during traffic spikes. Cost per task as a pass/fail metric

Cost should be an eval metric with a threshold, computed on the same runs as accuracy. Don't treat it as a bill you check afterwards. The unit is the task, not the token: a cheaper model that needs more turns or more retries can cost more for each problem it solves (
Cost per solved task (not price per token)
). The response's
block reports input, output and cache token counts. Multiply them by the per-token prices, then divide total spend by the number of tasks in the run.

A cost threshold is relative to something. The ticket-routing example sets two thresholds side by side: 95% accuracy over 100 tests, and a 50% average reduction in cost per classification compared with the current routing method. In the insurance-claims cookbook, a baseline agent scored 10/10 at about $0.29 per task. Because a mislabelled claim costs more than the inference saved, the team kept the accuracy requirement at 10/10 and treated cost as the number to push down. A configuration that saves money but drops a case fails, however cheap it is.
Why would a single eval run be weak evidence that a cheaper configuration meets its cost threshold?
Exam trap
When comparing configurations, the one with the lower price per token is the cheaper one.
Why is that wrong?

Quantifying safety and security as checkable rates

"The assistant should be safe" is a hope, not a criterion. Even fuzzy goals like ethics and safety can be expressed as rates: the share of outputs, over a stated number of trials, that a stated detector flags. A good safety criterion names three things: the detector (a content filter), the sample size (10,000 trials) and the ceiling (fewer than 0.1% flagged). Severity needs the same treatment. "90% of errors would cause inconvenience, not egregious error" is computable only once you have written down what counts as inconvenient and what counts as egregious.

A security metric is computed the same way. The difference is that you first have to define what counts as a successful attack, specifically enough that code or a grader can decide it. Start from the threat model, because there are two. In jailbreaks and direct prompt injection, the user is the adversary and writes inputs meant to get around your guardrails. In indirect prompt injection, the user is trusted, but Claude reads third-party content (web pages, emails, documents, tool results) that contains adversarial instructions. Each one needs its own adversarial test set and its own success condition. The metric is then the attack success rate: the share of attack attempts that meet that condition.
Write success conditions as observable outcomes, never as "the model seemed manipulated":
A harmlessness screen is a model call that labels incoming input as harmful or not before it reaches the main conversation. Structured outputs force it to return a fixed label, such as a boolean
, so code can compare it with the known answer. An attack succeeds when a known-harmful input comes back labelled safe.
For data handling, an attack succeeds when the output uses or shares a detail the instructions said to withhold.
For agents, an attack succeeds when the end state shows the forbidden effect, checked against environment state rather than the transcript's wording.
The authentication-bypass task below shows the agent version. Its graders spell out what "secure" means: deterministic tests that reject empty and null passwords, a static security scan with
, and a state check that the security log recorded an
event. If any of them fails, the fix fails, however convincing the agent's explanation sounds.
An agent eval task whose graders define security success as passing tests, a clean security scan and an auth_blocked log event
yaml
Apply it to your own work
Pick one guardrail in a system you know. What exactly would have to appear in the output, a log or the environment for you to record an attack against it as successful?
Exam trap
Safety is a qualitative judgement and can't be given a numeric pass/fail threshold.
Why is that wrong?
